title: Malawax
author: Chef Amina Hassan
desc: A soft, slightly sweet Somali pancake-bread, thicker and more tender than canjeero, traditionally rolled around a filling of sugar and ghee or dipped into savory stew.
longDesc: Malawax sits somewhere between a pancake and a flatbread, its batter enriched with a touch of sugar that gives it a gentle sweetness, and it's traditionally rolled up while warm, either plain, with a smear of ghee and sugar, or alongside a savory suqaar for a satisfying contrast.
ingredients: 2 tbsp ghee or butter, melted, plus more for serving
steps: Dissolve the yeast in a little of the warm milk with a pinch of the sugar and let sit for 10 minutes.
Combine the flour, remaining sugar, and salt in a bowl.
Whisk in the egg, yeast mixture, and remaining milk until you have a smooth, medium-thick batter.
Heat a lightly oiled non-stick pan over medium heat.
Pour a ladle of batter into the pan, swirling gently to spread into a round.
Cook for 2-3 minutes until the top sets and bubbles appear, then flip and cook the other side briefly.
Brush with melted ghee and serve warm, rolled or folded.
chefTips: Malawax is thicker than canjeero and, unlike canjeero, is traditionally flipped and cooked on both sides.
A touch of sugar in the batter is what gives malawax its gentle sweetness, distinguishing it from savory canjeero.
Serve warm with ghee and sugar for a classic breakfast, or alongside a savory stew for contrast.
commonMistakes: Making the batter too thin, losing the soft, pancake-like thickness that defines malawax.
Overcooking, which can dry out the tender crumb.
Skipping the rest time, which allows the yeast and gluten to develop properly.
storage: Refrigerate stacked and wrapped for up to 2 days.
reheating: Warm briefly in a dry pan.
healthBenefits: A good source of protein from the milk and egg.
culturalNote: Malawax is a comforting staple across Somali households, its gentle sweetness making it especially popular with children and a common feature of family breakfasts.
